Student Features

Kyra Lesmerises

SoC '26 - SURG

Kyra Lesmerises

Please provide a brief summary of your research: For my research, I studied female stand-up comedians and their style of comedy, and also the material they talked about in their sets. I attended many stand-up shows in the Chicago area, and took notes on the jokes of these comedians. I also interviewed four female comedians, and asked them their thoughts on their comedy career, and how they believe women are perceived in comedy. My research was focused on if women used anecdotal storytelling more frequently, and if their material was more frequently related to dating/sex/relationships. I concluded through analysis of the jokes I heard that storytelling was used more frequently among female stand-ups, while women did not talk about dating/sex/relationships more than they did about other topics. My interviews corroborated this info, with the comedians I interviewed stating that women are perceived as talking about those topics more, even when male comedians talk about those topics all the time, highlighting the biases and stereotypes that come with being a woman in comedy.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular? I took a stand-up class during winter quarter of my junior year, and I really enjoyed it. Near the end of the class, I thought about my stand-up and the style I leaned toward and the topics I talked about. I then thought about the differences between the performances of the female students in my class versus the male students, and began to wonder about the trends in stand-up done by women.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly? I had never done research before, and it seemed like a really interesting opportunity to explore my passion in a lot more depth. I also thought that my major and my passions didn't really lend itself to research, but once I learned that I could do a creative research project, I decided to apply. It seemed like a way to stretch my brain in a way that I hadn't before.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained? It was tricky to get started at the beginning. I knew what I had outlined in my proposal, but when it came time to actually start, I got nervous about reaching out to comedians and interviewing them. However, once I made my first contact and had a great experience interviewing them, I became a lot more confident, and even excited to conduct these interviews. I really honed my interviewing skills, specifically when it came to crafting my questions to get specific and really interesting answers.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? If you are a in a major similar to mine, don't think you can't do research! If you have an interest, you can find a way to ask a research question and then study it. When you are really passionate about your topic, the research doesn't feel like work, but rather a really cool opportunity to learn more about this topic that you enjoy so much!

Charlie Du

McCormick '29 - URAP

Charlie Du

Please provide a brief summary of your research: My research focuses on forecasting dynamical systems, which are systems that change over time, such as vibrations in structures, weather patterns, financial markets, and the spread of diseases. Traditional models often struggle to take full advantage of the large amounts of data available today, and they rarely tell us how reliable their predictions are. To address this, our work develops a new data-driven approach using neural operators, a modern machine learning technique that learns how entire systems evolve over time. Beyond predicting future behavior, our approach also estimates how confident those predictions are by drawing on statistical ideas such as quantile regression and Bayesian methods. This allows the model to capture both errors in the data and limitations in the model itself, producing predictions along with confidence intervals.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular? AI is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily lives, so I was interested in doing something related to machine learning because machine learning is what we use to train AI.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly? What drew me to interdisciplinary research is that the problems I find most interesting rarely fit inside a single field. My work on uncertainty quantification for dynamical systems sits at the intersection of machine learning, statistics, and the physical sciences, and it only works because ideas from each inform the others. Coming from computer engineering, I enjoy moving between the theory and the implementation, and I have found that the most useful insights often come from borrowing a concept from one area and applying it somewhere it was not originally meant to go. 

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained? Yes, research takes a lot of time, but it is rewarding in the end. I have developed strong analytical skills, learning how to break down complex problems, question my assumptions, and work through challenges methodically when results do not turn out as expected. I have also become much better at communicating technical ideas, whether that means writing clearly for a paper, presenting my work to people outside my field, or explaining my reasoning to mentors and peers. Beyond the technical side, research has taught me patience and persistence, since progress and results often come slowly.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? Do not wait until you feel fully qualified to do research! Reach out to as many professors as you can. Read about their work first, and if their research aligns with your interests, send a short, genuine email explaining what drew you to their lab and ask to set up a meeting. Research is where you learn, and showing curiosity and a willingness to put in the work often matters more than having all the right experience up front.

Rosa Saavedra

WCAS '28 - AYURG + URAP

Rosa Saavedra

Please provide a brief summary of your research: My research through the Lab for Accelerating Clinical Technologies (ACT) began with FoodSteps, a behavioral health intervention app designed to support individuals experiencing food insecurity and binge eating through one-on-one coaching and additional resources aimed at reducing binge episodes. Because food insecurity is associated with a higher prevalence of binge eating and poorer overall health outcomes, my independent research focused on how clinical terminology (specifically the term “binge eating”) is perceived by diverse groups, particularly individuals experiencing food insecurity. I also explored alternative descriptors that may be more reflective of lived experience and preferred by participants. The broader goal of this research is to improve self-help resources, increase access to care, and enhance engagement with interventions such as FoodSteps among underserved populations.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular? Growing up, I visited family in Venezuela nearly every summer until conditions in the country became too dangerous. It placed me in a unique in-between space: while my own family was relatively stable, I was regularly exposed to the realities of food insecurity and limited access to resources affecting many people around us. Seeing how these challenges impacted individuals I cared about, from an early age, I was curious about how health issues disproportionately affect underserved populations and the broader effects of food insecurity on physical and mental health. At the same time, witnessing a close friend struggle with an eating disorder in high school gave me firsthand insight into how deeply these conditions can affect not only the individual, but also their relationships and overall well-being. Together, these experiences shaped my interest in understanding the intersection of food insecurity, eating behaviors, and health outcomes. When applying to URAP, I saw in the ACT lab an opportunity to explore these intersecting interests. They also drew me to the potential of telemedicine and technology-based interventions to improve access to care for individuals who may otherwise face barriers to treatment.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly? As a Neuroscience major, much of my prior research experience from high school and my time at Northwestern before applying to URAP was primarily wet lab-based. Through these prior experiences I had grown familiar with working with various wet lab instruments as well as analyzing quantitative data. What initially struck me about the opportunity in the ACT lab at the time, aside from its mission, was its use of qualitative and mixed methods data (fusion of both qualitative and quantitative). The concept of pulling out conclusions from words felt so foreign to me and going into it, I was skeptical and curious about how it would be done.

In my time in the lab I have learned that qualitative data provides context and answers that quantitative data alone can not fully capture. While numbers and graphs are powerful tools for identifying patterns and outcomes, examining participants’ stories, struggles, and experiences with health interventions has offered a deeper understanding of how individuals engage with care and develop confidence in their ability to change their outcomes. In my independent project, I saw firsthand how integrating different methods can lead to more nuanced, patient-centered research. This experience broadened my perspective on research and bridged the gap between science and people.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained? I have been incredibly blessed in my research experiences thus far. Throughout my time in research, I have benefited from a strong support system of undergraduate research advisors (shoutout Megan!), knowledgeable and patient principal investigators, and collaborative lab communities that have encouraged my growth (and encouraged that I make mistakes!). At the same time, research has not been void of challenges. Balancing coursework with lab responsibilities requires intentional time management, realistic expectations, and clear communication about the time and energy I can commit on a weekly basis. Over time, I have become much better at managing competing priorities, adapting to unexpected setbacks, and asking for help when needed. However, engaging in research has also opened doors to opportunities I may not have otherwise had. Through my involvement in research, I have presented posters, gained manuscript-writing experience, and even written grants, such as for AYURG. These experiences have given me skills that transcend the lab environment. I have learned how to communicate complex ideas to diverse audiences, collaborate with people who are also passionate about research, and become more comfortable stepping into unfamiliar or challenging situations. In many ways, research has pushed me to grow in ways I never anticipated.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? My biggest piece of advice would be to take full advantage of the resources your school provides. The research advisors were super helpful throughout my experience and can be great guides when navigating opportunities, applications, and uncertainty. I would also encourage students to be open to research outside of what they initially expect or even outside of their major. As a Neuroscience major, stepping into psychology and behavioral health research exposed me to entirely new ways of thinking, methodologies, and questions that I otherwise would not have encountered. Being willing to try something unfamiliar taught me a lot skill wise, and ultimately broadened my perspective as a researcher and a person.

 

Shirley Yang

WCAS '26 - AYURG

Shirley Yang

Please provide a brief summary of your research: My research investigates the island effect, a phenomenon in which certain English sentences (e.g., “What does John know the student that saw?”) are judged as unacceptable. Using an online experiment, I tested whether these effects can be solely explained by information structural packaging. The results suggest towards a conclusion that information structure cannot be the only cause of island effects.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular? The project grew out of my final paper for an upper-level Syntax course, which was a literature overview on the island effect. I wanted to explore the topic a little bit further by designing and carrying out my own independent research project.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly? In classes, I often just "passively" learn theories as established knowledge. Research interested me because it gave me the opportunity to actively test my own ideas and questions while learning from faculty mentors how to conduct professional research.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained? I faced many challenges in defining a strong research question and carrying out the experiments, but I learned a great deal through this project. I am now becoming more and more like a professional researcher by learning how to write grant proposals, submit conference abstracts, and present my work at conferences.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? Don’t be afraid to talk to professors and ask questions about ideas that genuinely interest you. For logistics or funding-related questions, don’t hesitate to reach out to your advisors and the Office of Undergraduate Research! 

Juniper Shelley

SESP '27 - Circumnav

Juniper Shelley

Please provide a brief summary of your research: This summer, I explored how men in different cultural contexts experience loneliness, masculinity, and emotional connection, and how community-based programs can help address the recent uptick in male isolation. I worked with an international nonprofit called the ManKind Project, which facilitates men’s conversation groups in over two dozen countries. My goal was to create actionable recommendations that will allow the ManKind Project to improve its adaptability across cultural contexts.

My research will took me to Mexico, South Africa, Sweden, Japan, and Australia. I chose these locations because they represent very different cultural models of masculinity, from highly egalitarian societies to more traditional ones. The ManKind Project has thrived in some of these countries, and struggled in others. By making comparisons between these locations, I learned what kinds of approaches are the most effective at facilitating community around the world.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? Be open minded to changing your approach as you go. This project is certainly not what I imagined I would be working on when I began doing research for this grant. However, it quickly revealed itself as the most accessible and relevant topic within my general interest area. For other students that are interested in independent research, I recommend that you start with a big idea, and let the resources that are available guide your specific research plan.

Final reflections (from her blog): I wish I could express properly how thankful I am. In such a short time I have traveled to 13 countries on 5 continents. I have observed and participated in male community groups in 6 countries. I’ve gone on 15 hikes, mostly in Australia, Switzerland, and South Africa. I’ve been surfing in Australia, seen the World Cup in Mexico, had the best udon of my life in Japan, and swam in the Baltic Sea in Sweden. I’ve made friends all over the world: In Sydney, I met up with an Australian girl who I met at a hostel in Belgium, and in Copenhagen I spent a day with four German boys I met swimming in the canals. I’ve visited 13 museums. I’ve gotten my hair cut short in a small village in France, spent a day driving around Cape Town with middle-aged Italians, and seen a Bruno Mars concert in Amsterdam. And, I’ve completed over 60 interviews with men all over the world.

These 70 days have been foundational, and I predict that what I’ve learned will stay with me for the rest of my life. I’m going back to school feeling like a braver, more curious, more informed person.

I have a new found invigoration for what’s next. This trip has taught me that I have control over my own experience. And while it’s unlikely that I’ll ever have another opportunity like this, I’m going home with the comforting feeling that my next step will be just as fulfilling as long as I’m there.

 

Caleb Eng

WCAS '28 - URAP

Caleb Eng

Please provide a brief summary of your research. Professor Shiffer-Sebba and I investigated how online social interactions are shaped by wealth using publicly posted data from decentralized social systems that are tied to crypto wallets. I was personally responsible for developing robust scripts in Python that pulled the data from online, and I did much of the preliminary analysis.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?The ability for behaviors to be learned from networks is particularly interesting, yet very hard to measure. This project was a unique opportunity to combine data gathered from both financial and social inputs and study how the two interact in a clear empirical environment.

What made you interested in pursuing research more broadly? Someday I would like to pursue a PhD in economics. As such, pursuing research is helpful to get a glimpse for what activities I might be engaged in in the future.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained?Coming into the project my experience with research was minimal. Throughout the course of the project I learned so many technical skills such as developing my coding ability, analyzing data using regression, and how to specifically analyze data from social networks.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? Make sure that research is something that excites you! I'm blessed to be able to say that I was on a project that I genuinely enjoyed.

What was your favorite childhood story (written, spoken, or film)? I really liked the Swiss Family Robinson movie when I was young

 

Jalil Hemphill

McCormick '29 - URAP

Jalil Hemphill

 

Please provide a brief summary of your research. DNA methylation is a process in biology in which chemical tags are added to parts of DNA affecting whether certain genes are turned on or off. The effects created by this process can sometimes lead to effects like aging and other health risks such as disease. Looking specifically at people with Schizophrenia, these tags can be used to create biological clocks that help to predict these different effects of DNA methylation. My project focuses on expanding past the previous models used and building new clocks that can better predict these effects utilizing other models including elastic-net regression.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?Machine learning is a immensely growing field currently. It is being applied in almost every field now. Working with the large amount of data in biology and applying this into a complex field like epigenetics really interested me as there was so much for me to learn. Understanding how different types of models can be applied to fields like biology and neuroscience is fascinating as the human brain is something still not fully understood and so complex.

What made you interested in pursuing research more broadly? Someday I would like to pursue a PhD in economics. As such, pursuing research is helpful to get a glimpse for what activities I might be engaged in in the future.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly? Going into my first year of university, research was something that had always interested me as it is making a real impact in a field. Seeing all the work different professors do is inspiring, and there is always something new to learn. Combining my major Computer Science with a field like biology and seeing the intersection and differences they can have is fascinating. I knew no matter the project I worked on it would allow for a great amount of growth as a student early in my career.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained? As somebody with a mostly CS background, I did not have the biology background to fully understand everything at the beginning. There was a lot of vocabulary and concepts I was not familiar with at first. Learning how to fully understand the models and the underlying statistics and biology concepts was something I have improved on. I worked on developing good questions to ask my mentor in order to better understand my project even more in-depth. Furthermore, I built my time management skills as I learned how to better balance the work I put into research with my classes and other commitments.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research? Be curious, ask as many questions as possible to experienced people in your field, but do not be afraid to dive in on your own. It can be overwhelming to be in a position where you do not fully understand everything going on, but if you work at it you will end up way better than you were before and fulfilled.

If your (speaking) voice were an instrument, what do you think it would be? Drums

 

Brookelyn Slonaker

SoC'26 (Communication Sciences & Disorders)

Brookelyn Slonaker

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My research evaluated the accuracy of common speech and language screeners in a diverse population of preschool age children. This is towards the goal of using one of these measures as a universal screening tool. We measured sensitivity (true positive) and specificity (true negative) of the screeners in comparison to at-risk decisions made by trained clinicians. In the results, we found discrepancies between clinician decisions and screener decisions- indicating inaccuracy. There was a particular trend toward false negatives, meaning that some screeners were under-diagnosing. This is a serious concern, since screeners are meant to cast a wide net- which is then narrowed by more in-depth assessments. This means that the accuracy of these screeners need to be improved before a universal screening measure can be developed.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I feel particularly drawn towards the pediatric population, having four younger siblings myself. I think it is vital that we make sure we are giving our children the best possible chance in life- and that includes accurate and early identification and treatment for communication disorders.

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
I was very nervous ahead of time, especially since I opted in for judging. But once I got there, I realized that all I was doing was telling people about something I am passionate about- disseminating information that needs to be heard. After that, I really enjoyed getting to tell people about these important findings and what they mean for the field.

I gave my presentation much more than I expected to. By the end of the session, I had been talking almost nonstop.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
Make sure you are presenting on a topic that you feel passionate about and that you think is important. When you do that, it's not difficult or scary at all, and everyone who listens to you will be able to tell how much you care about it.

What is something that you could give a 10 min presentation on right off the cuff?
Bears, specifically brown bears, specifically specifically Grizzly bears

What was a memorable interaction that you had on campus this week?
I saw my first baby bunny of the season, stood and stared at it for as long as possible.

 

Cooper Stringer

WCAS'26 (Biological Sciences)

Cooper Stringer

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
Our lab discovered a new protein in the fruit fly that has some interesting properties, especially relating to its trafficking. So to learn more about its functions and behavior, I designed a genetic tool that lets me control the timing, location, and level of our protein's expression across the fly. I then used this tool to measure the secretion and uptake of our protein in different tissues, and learned a lot about its regulation and possible applications.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I love learning how cells work together to give rise to tissues, and since my previous research experiences had been in cell culture, I wanted to broaden my experience by working with a model organism. Once I reached out to my current lab, I was told about this project-- a new protein is a notable find, especially in a system as well-characterized as Drosophila melanogaster, so I was excited to join on!

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
Getting to explain your research to a broad audience really challenges you to engage with your work in ways that you might not have before. I had to ask myself questions like, "what does my project mean for the field?", "why did I do my experiments in this order?", and "how do my results add up together towards one conclusion?"

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
The range of people who see your poster and want to learn more is surprising. I got to talk about biology with graduate students and faculty with years in the field, and undergrads and parents with almost no background. So the challenge is: how do you change your presentation to fit your audience individually, so that they can follow along without getting lost or bored? You don't want anybody walking away from your presentation thinking "Wow, that work must be impressive, because I didn't understand any of it." You want them to walk away thinking, "Wow, that work is impressive," BECAUSE they understand it.

What is something that you could give a 10 min presentation on right off the cuff?
The Kakapo of New Zealand: Evolution's Underdog

If your (speaking) voice were an instrument, what do you think it would be?
An oboe

What was your favorite childhood story (written, spoken, or film)?
The Adventures of Willy the Walking Pancake and Sebastian the Amazing Wonder-Pig

Nzubechukwu Nwafo

WCAS'26 (Biological Sciences & Global Health)

Nzubechukwu Nwafo

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My research focuses primarily on cardiac function, and the factors that contribute to it. We study the role of certain proteins using different methods of data analysis to track varying levels of cardiac efficiency.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I am interested the heart because it is central to human life. It has implications in all other bodily organs, and is integral to every process in the body. Since it is so vital to our being, new discoveries and improving knowledge on cardiac function fascinates me.

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
Presenting at the Expo was a good mix of professional and casual. It was nice to both share the work I have been doing and new learnings to family and friends, as well as present the complex experiment to judges in a more serious manner. I didn't expect for there to be such a wide range of topics presented by others at the Expo.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
I would advise others to make sure that they are interested in what they are researching, so that it's easy and enjoyable to talk about it with others who have varying levels of experience within your field.

 

Isaiah DeLeon

WCAS'25 (Linguistics & Psychology)

Isaiah DeLeon

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
I investigated the Gay Voice speech stereotype and created a web experiment testing if s-type sound features are part of that stereotype. Straight American actor Darren Criss was used as auditory and visual stimuli because of his famous portrayal of a gay character on Glee. Using visual primes in an experimental context can be tricky because facial expressions, hair styles, facial features, and other factors influence what social meaning we detect from the prime; since there existed a photo of Criss marrying his wife in real life and his character marrying a man on Glee, I used him to solve this problem. He was the source for straight and gay visual stimuli, and I used a neutral profile avatar as a control. Ultimately, there wasn't any support that the s-type sound feature I tested is not part of the Gay Voice stereotype, and the theoretical explanation is because specific phonetic features cn mean multiple different things and are used creatively to communicate (and perceive) complex identities in speech.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I've always liked learning about the mind sciences, but one of the most interesting things I learned in a linguistics class is that listeners; perception of a speaker's voice can actually change depending on their expectations of how they speak. When talking to someone of a specific race, gender, sexual orientation, or nationality, our expectations of how those groups talk can "override" how we sense their voices!

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
I truly had such a fun time. I have much experience with tabling and canvassing, so I was able to use that to have an engaging dialogue with people interested in my project.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
Have fun! It's easy to tell when someone is having fun presenting their research, and it allows people to deeply engage with your work!

 

 

 

 

Faith Do

WCAS'26 (Computer Science & Cognitive Science)

Faith Do

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
The TEAMS project at the SONIC Lab uses social networks analysis to model communication dynamics between small human-AI teams of 2-4. By applying RHEM and its associated covariates (i.e. variables), we can figure out which type of communication dynamic is most effective for producing a more productive or accurate team depending on the task.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
Human-AI and HCI has always been of interest to me, and after taking Professor Contractor's class in Social Networks Analysis, I was fascinated on how networks could be used to model these types of interactions.

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
A lot and a lot of talking! No surprises thankfully, but since networks is more of a niche topic I had to reexplain some of the basics many, many times.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
Gauging the level of knowledge or the specialty of the person you are speaking to is insanely helpful. Knowing how much they know about your research can help you speak more on their level, whether that be more generally or with as much detail as even you know. And knowing their specialty can help you relate your research to something they are more familiar with.

What would you name a boat if you had one?
Splashy

What is something that you could give a 10 min presentation on right off the cuff?
I know everything ever about the Barbie Cinematic Universe (BCU), not like the recent Barbie movie (but that too) but the old Barbie movies made by Mattel to sell the dolls. I know all the movies, the characters, plots, release dates, how they link together, etc etc. I'm ready to go at any moment about this.

If your (speaking) voice were an instrument, what do you think it would be?
Bass

What was your favorite childhood story (written, spoken, or film)?
My mom tells me I was obsessed with the book Goodnight Moon. I also loved Blue's Clues

What was a memorable interaction that you had on campus this week?
Did a jig with a stranger

 

 

 

Kumiko Long

SoC'28 (Human Communication Sciences)

Kumiko Long

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
I work in Dr. Rodriguez-Contreras's Neonate Neuroscience lab in which we explore the impact of hypoxia, or oxygen deficiency in the tissues, on neurovascular development using rat models. We are searching for observable signs of hypoxia-induced nervous system dysfunction by tracking weight, decision making, sensorimotor behavior, and hearing. Since premature infants commonly experience hypoxic episodes, we aim to use our findings to inform the potential hazards of prematurity and hypoxia in general.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
This lab was matched with me as part of the Early Research Experience Award program. With my goal of entering the audiology field, the hearing-related aspects of this study are extremely compelling to me. Through this project, I gained valuable experience with conducting auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing and learned more about how our hearing mechanisms function.

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
Presenting at the Expo reminded me of an elevated version of a middle school science fair. I didn't expect there to be such a variety of presentation topics from so many different fields!

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
My biggest tip would be to really consider your audience and their level of understanding (especially if you are dealing with technical topics). It's helpful to practice as though you are explaining to a little kid and work from there.

What was your favorite childhood story (written, spoken, or film)?
Harold and the Purple Crayon

What was a memorable interaction that you had on campus this week?
Playing a show with my band!

 

 

Dylan Stone

WCAS'27 (Biological Sciences & Religious Studies)

Dylan Stone

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My research explores how disrupting circadian rhythms impacts gut inflammation, using a mouse model of ulcerative colitis. I induced colitis in mice by giving them dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) in their drinking water, and compared disease severity between wild-type mice and mice with a Clock Δ19 mutation, a genetic alteration that disrupts their circadian clock. We tracked clinical symptoms daily, including weight loss, stool consistency, and rectal bleeding, and statistically analyzed the progression of disease. The goal was to investigate whether a misaligned circadian rhythm makes colitis worse; a question with real-world relevance for shift workers and patients with IBD.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I’ve lived with Crohn’s disease for years, so I’ve always been curious about the factors that trigger flare-ups. Beyond the immune system, I started wondering how daily habits, like sleep and eating schedules, might influence inflammation. That’s what drew me to this project. The idea that something as fundamental as your sleep could change the severity of disease felt both personal and scientifically compelling. This project gave me a chance to investigate that link in a concrete way using tools from immunology, genetics, and physiology.

What was it like presenting at the Expo? Anything that you didn't expect?
Presenting at the Expo was a really cool experience. I was a little nervous at first, but once I started talking to people, it felt more like a conversation than a presentation. What surprised me most was how genuinely curious people were, even those without a science background. I got a lot of thoughtful questions, which made the experience more engaging than I expected. I was really grateful that my project connected with so many people, and it was a nice surprise to be recognized with the Audience Choice Award for the afternoon poster session.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at the Expo one day?
My biggest tip is to focus on the story behind your science – why your research matters and how it connects to real people. Simplify your figures and avoid jargon so anyone walking by can understand the core idea. Also, practice explaining your project out loud to friends who aren’t in your field, that helped me catch things that didn’t make sense. Don’t be afraid to show your passion for your work – the best work comes from a genuine personal interest.

What was your favorite childhood story (written, spoken, or film)?
Toy Story

 

Jack Ryan

WCAS'27 (Physics & Integrated Science Program)

Jack Ryan

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My research in the Geraci lab looks to implement a Horizontal Fiber Interferometer (HIFO) within the ARIADNE experiment. Within ARIADNE, an experiment searching for a well-motivated dark matter candidate the Axion, a rotating source mass is utilized to generate a pseudo magnetic field carried by the axion, affecting hyper-polarized helium-3 gas. Due to the design and nature of the experiment, the source mass will have a slight wobble to its motion, but this wobble must not exceed 75 microns. A method to detect this, the HIFO, is necessary to readout the displacement of the rotor in situ, under cryogenic vacuum conditions reaching 4K and 10E-6 atm. The HIFO is a laser interferometer which shines perpendicular to the rotating source mass and utilizes a metric known as visibility to detect the wobble. During my past research, it was found that there is a direct one to one relationship between measured visibility and distance from the rotating mass. My past work has also shown this direct relationship can be utilized as a "ruler," precisely measuring the displacement of the source mass on the order of several microns. Over the past year and a half, my research has pursued designing, implementing, testing, and utilizing this HIFO to accurately measure the displacement of the source mass for eventual data taking experimental runs of the larger ARIADNE experiment.

Coming to Northwestern, I knew I was interested in being involved with physics research. As I was looking into different labs, the Geraci group within the Center for Fundamental Physics caught my eye as it had many tabletop physics experiments probing the limits of our knowledge of physics. One of these experiments was ARIADNE, looking for a theorized dark matter candidate the Axion. The idea that dark matter research, one of physics most pressing questions, was being conducting right on campus immediately caught my eye. Within ARIADNE, the HIFO was a project that looked to solve an issue the large experiment possessed, while utilizing ideas accessible to me as a new undergraduate.

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
A subset of Parkinson's patients face increased aggregation of alpha-synuclein due to loss of activity of Glucosylceramidase (GCase). Our project focuses on increasing GCase activity through a multivalent Spherical Nucleic Acid (SNA) platform, where we used GCase as the protein core and attached Folate and Transferrin on GCase. In some of the countries I visited, “indigenous” referred to whoever settled the land first. In others, it seemed to correlate with the largest ethnic group, or even the group most represented in government. It was fascinating to compare these distinctions and learn how they influence the everyday lives of different groups in the same community.

Will Yuen

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My focus was pre-clinical research concerning a promising potential therapeutic to alleviate Renal Ischemic Reperfusion Injury (IRI), an unavoidable injury in the organ transplant setting. There are currently no effective treatments for this inevitable injury. To do this my lab and I developed a novel in vitro cold hypoxia and reperfusion protocol to best model transplant related IRI in tubular epithelial cells (TECs), the main target of this type of injury. This involved subjecting TECs to 6h of cold hypoxia followed by a designated time of reperfusion (incubation in fresh media at 37C). My research confirmed that this model properly mimicked renal IRI in vitro by confirming the presence of inflammation, kidney injury, and cell death in TECs via qPCR, flow cytometry, and fluorescence staining assays across multiple time points (0h, 2h, 16h, and 24h of reperfusion) compared to control. I then investigated the effect of the potential therapeutic on these same factors. The therapeutic is an siRNA knockdown of XBP1, a vital transcription factor in the ER stress pathway that results in inflammation. Compared to non-transfected cells, TECs transfected with XBP1 siRNA displayed less inflammation, kidney injury, and cell death imaged/quantified via the same assays used previously. This emphasized that the knockdown of XBP1 in TECs is a promising potential therapeutic to alleviate IRI.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I found it particularly compelling that this type of injury (IRI) is quite unavoidable during/after transplantation and that we somehow have not developed any effective solutions to this injury. Please provide a brief summary of your research.
This past summer, I investigated the relationship between spatial cognition and global vs. local processing of undergraduate students. To measure spatial cognition, I used results from undergraduate student performance of the block design task (BDT). In this task, participants were provided a 2D pattern and had to use 3D blocks called SCUBEs to replicate them, where each block would consist of red faces, white faces, and faces which were half red and half right. Performances were scored through a system I developed, which took factors such overall erroneous actions and performance efficiency into consideration. It was then correlated with participants’ global vs local processing, which is a measure of the degree of holistic processing in comparison to their level of detail orientedness. This was measured through a survey which participants were given, where they were provided a series shapes composed of smaller but different shapes (eg: a square made up of a series of small triangles). Participants then had to indicate whether they thought the image better resembled the larger shape, which would suggest global processing, or the smaller shapes, which would suggest local processing.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I was first introduced to the use of SCUBEs to better understand spatial cognition in a DevSci Networking event, where the graduate students working on this project presented their work. I found the SCUBEs themselves to be quite fascinating, as they have been engineered to detect movement in order to more efficiently and effectively measure participant performance. The use of technology to better understand human behaviour is something that has always intrigued me, as its rapid development is causing it to become increasingly integrated into our lives. Furthermore, spatial cognition was something which I was still quite unfamiliar with at the time, which was why I thought it would be extremely meaningful to further explore this aspect of cognitive science/psychology. The findings from this research can also be applied in educational settings to help improve STEM learning, which provided a strong sense of purpose for what I was doing.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly?
I believe that research is a path which can impact both me and the people around me quite significantly. As for the long run, the findings of my research can be applied in such a variety of fields and thus impact a very wide and diverse range of people. More specifically, doing interdisciplinary research can be especially meaningful because it allows for the questions I investigate to connect more closely to the real world. Factors which may not directly relate to the academic field I am focus on can be more easily taken into consideration and therefore maximize the potential it has to impact people.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained?
My experience with research so far has been great. Summer research specifically has allowed me to grow from both academically and personally. From an academic standpoint, I was able to strengthen my understanding of exploratory psychological research. In the past, I was taught to follow a strict procedure with a clear question to be answered. However, I have learned that doing so doesn’t allow for the flexibility necessary to account for the complexity and broad range of factors that can influence the variable to be investigated. In regards to this study specifically, I had the opportunity to explore the various methods of processing the same data. I also had to learn how to make procedural decisions, run experiments, and present my research in various forms. As for my personal growth, my summer experience has strengthened my integrity, proactivity, as well as flexibility. Please provide a brief summary of your research.
I spent the summer studying Chicago Catholics who attend Mass in Latin. Until the late 1960s, rituals in the Roman Catholic Church, including Sunday Mass, were largely in Latin. The 1960s brought a series of monumental changes to Catholic way of life, including to aesthetics and approaches to various doctrines. This shift culminated in the introduction of a new Mass: one that could be said in vernacular languages and which had removed many of the prayers and rituals that had been in use for centuries. While majority of the world's 1 billion Catholics have adopted this way of being Catholic, a small minority preserved the old Mass, and its members have created a unique subculture within global Catholicism. Latin Mass attendees are known for being liturgically, doctrinally and politically conservative. My project explored why they are a part of this community, how they think about various church teachings and contemporary issues, and how they think families and society should be structured. My methods included a survey that drew about 500 participants, interviews that drew about 150 interested participants, interviews with priests, and frequenting churches that offer the Latin Mass in Chicago. Traditional Catholicism has important implications for the Catholic Church, but also for our diverse and secular society. Much like Evangelical Protestantism created the Southern Bible Belt and Muslim immigration is shifting the culture in Michigan and Minneapolis, the steady growth of traditional Catholics will also impact the communities their members inhabit.

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My research this summer focused on determining whether mixtures of peptide amphiphiles (PAs) with the peptide sequences A2G2 and V2A2 would result in molecularly mixed or phase-separated (non-mixing) supramolecular nanofiber assemblies. To test this, I utilized variable temperature polarized light microscopy (VT-PLM) to record the temperature at which PA fiber assemblies transitioned into spherical micelles. This transition temperature was denoted by the complete loss of birefringence signal, produced by anisotropic nanofiber assemblies, indicating a complete transition to isotropic spherical micelles.

Based on previous work, the A2G2 peptide sequence is known to form weak β-sheets that produce less cohesive nanofibers, leading to lower transition temperatures. In contrast, the V2A2 sequence is known to form strong β-sheets and more cohesive nanofibers, resulting in higher transition temperatures. Thus, increases in mol % composition of A2G2-based PAs mixed with V2A2-based PAs were expected to decrease cohesion within fiber nanostructures and therefore decrease the transition temperature. This trend was seen in my past work on mixtures of A2G2E2 with V2A2E2 PAs and A2G2E4-GIKVAV with V2A2E4-GIKVAV PAs, which indicated some degree of mixing between the PA pairs.

I chose to further analyze this trend by altering the equivalents of NaOH added to PA mixtures of the A2G2E4-GIKVAV with V2A2E4-GIKVAV PAs, which were originally prepared with 4 equivalents of NaOH. This mixture was selected in particular to better analyze the effect of epitopes like GIKVAV on the mixing of PAs. As greater equivalents of NaOH tend to reduce cohesion within a fiber assembly and therefore reduce the transition temperature, I was curious to see if the same transition temperature trend would persist in mixtures of 3 and 3.5 equivalents of NaOH as well. Under VT-PLM, the same trend in transition temperature was observed for all equivalents of NaOH, noted by a more rapid decrease in birefringence signal intensity with increasing % A2G2E4-GIKVAV. In addition, for the 30% and 50% A2G2E4-GIKVAV samples at all NaOH equivalents, there appeared to be multiple inflection points along the heating profiles; however, these inflections became less distinct with greater equivalents of NaOH. These inflection points suggested that there was a two-phase mixture at intermediate compositions of the two PAs, i.e., the appearance of a miscibility gap at lower equivalents of NaOH. Therefore, this further confirmed that rather than PA mixtures forming either fully phase-separated or completely molecularly mixed fiber assemblies, there seemed to be an upper limit on the degree of mixing between the different PAs.

To add a little context for the photos - this is a photo of the birefringence signal detected from various fiber assembly mixtures of peptide amphiphiles under a polarized light microscope (PLM).

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
I was investigating how A549s, a patient derived lung cancer cell line, essentially hijack the circadian clock. Every cell in our body has a circadian rhythm, and we can visualize how long a cell's circadian period lasts in a device called the LumiCycle. There have been numerous studies investigating the relationship between circadian disruption (via shift work) and the development of cancer. Previous research by Dr. Clara Peek showed a bidirectional interaction between HIF-1a (a protein involved in the cellular response to low oxygen conditions) and BMAL1 (a core circadian clock component). Since tumor cells are naturally in low oxygen conditions, this relationship is pathologically relevant. Other scientists showed that circadian disruption leads to lung tumorigenesis, but we were investigating the opposite pathway - that being how A549s take over the circadian clock to benefit their growth and proliferation . My goal was to treat cells with different drugs that worked on our proposed signaling pathway and measure the length of the cell's circadian period.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I didn't have a particular interest in circadian biology until I took Bio 203, where we briefly went over how the circadian clock works. From there, I knew I wanted to work in a circadian lab. I had a previous interest in muscle physiology and injury repair, which is the main focus of the Peek lab and my initial reason for joining. When I arrived, one of the research techs, Adam Steffeck, mentioned that he needed help with the lab's lung cancer project. Although lung cancer and muscle physiology share few commonalities, the shared circadian component was my main motivation for helping with this project. From there, I began training in the lab and was ready to commit to the project full time when summer rolled around.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly?
I knew I wanted to start doing research because of my classes. I always found everything we learned so interesting, but never felt like I could fully grasp how these concepts applied to a real world setting. Techniques always seem practical when learning about them in lecture, but I wanted to experience the scientific process myself. I wanted to see how the things we learned failed, understand why they failed and make judgement calls as to what the next move should be to push the project forward. I saw research as a way to bring the content we cover to fruition, which was my main motivation to get involved.

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained?
I've loved my experience so far, but I can't say that every moment has been easy. Seeing your experiments that you've planned and set up for weeks fail because of reasons outside your control can be frustrating, and you have to learn to come back and think about your own work critically. I think the trickiest part is being able to ask the right questions at the right times. If you didn't get the result you wanted, was it because of a procedural error? Or is something mechanistic? Please provide a brief summary of your research.
Anterior temporal lobectomy (ATL) involves the surgical resection of left or right medial temporal lobe (MTL) structures to control seizures in 80% of patients with medication-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). MTL supports the formation and retrieval of memories for past experiences, so the benefits associated with ATL must be balanced with the risks of memory decline. Currently, presurgical memory lateralization relies on an invasive procedure called the Wada test, which can be inaccurate, particularly in younger children or those with developmental delays. This project aims to improve memory outcomes in pediatric TLE patients by using fMRI to determine memory lateralization prior to left or right ATL. To achieve this, we designed two memory tasks to be performed in-scanner, one examining associative memory and one examining naturalistic event memory. In healthy participants, we hypothesize bilateral MTL activation during the performance of both tasks. In patients with left or right TLE, we hypothesize greater activation lateralized to the non-epileptic MTL. Now, we are leading pilot testing of the memory tasks and subsequent data collection in healthy children and adolescents. Once we analyze the data, we plan to recommend one or both tasks to be paired with fMRI and employed in the presurgical evaluation of pediatric TLE patients. We further plan to pair the tasks with intracranial EEG during presurgical monitoring to examine the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying fMRI effects. We hope the findings of this project indicate that our clinical memory task method can replace the Wada test for patients being considered for ATL.

My research investigated how two proteins, dynein and ZYG-8, work together to promote proper spindle assembly during meiosis in C. elegans eggs. Meiosis is a type of cell division that creates eggs (oocytes) and sperm. Proper spindle assembly is vital for proper chromosome segregation during meiosis, which is needed to produce viable sex cells. Although structures known as centrosomes organize spindles during mitosis, they are absent in oocyte meiosis. Recent research at the Wignall Lab shows that these acentrosomal spindles are formed and stabilized by a variety of proteins in C. elegans oocytes, which are found in similar forms (homologs) in humans. Two of these proteins are dynein and ZYG-8, but their interactions with each other–if there are any–were still unknown. Therefore, my goal was to investigate how these two proteins might interact to assemble and maintain proper acentrosomal spindles, and promote proper chromosome segregation during oocyte meiosis.

When I first came across the research at the Wignall Lab, I was marveled by their findings and ongoing projects. As a Pre-Med interested in molecular biology and OB-Gyn, investigating factors that contribute to the formation of viable oocytes immediately piqued my interest. Dr. Sadie Wignall and her graduate students’ research are providing a broader and more detailed understanding of proper spindle formation, which is a step towards understanding the underlying causes of birth defects and miscarriages in humans. One of the graduate students at the lab, Emily Czajkowski, needed help with her research. Please provide the tile and a brief summary of your research/conference presentation.
Title: Modeling Individual Sleep Needs from Wearable-Device Data An individual’s natural sleep and wake cycle plays a critical role in nearly every aspect of their daily life. There are currently thought to be two processes that interact to regulate one’s sleep/wake cycle: a sleep homeostat, which depends on the amount of time you have been awake; and the circadian rhythm, an internal 24-hour molecular clock present in nearly every cell of the body. Both processes differ between individuals, whether that’s from a decision to pull an all-nighter one day or from a genetic inclination towards being an “early bird” or a “night owl”. This project focuses on building a model that can predict how particular sleep disruptions impact an individual’s sleep cycle, as well as their ability to recover from these disruptions. These processes have been studied and modeled using mathematical equations, which I was able to rewrite as more biologically realistic equations, and implement as code, resulting in a computational “two-process” model that can simulate a theoretical sleep-wake cycle with disruptions. Once we have a model that can use an individual’s data to predict their optimal sleep despite disruptions, it could be used in the field of sleep medicine to identify and address parameters affecting those with sleep disorders. Given its versatility, the model could also be used by anyone experiencing disruptions due to travel, social events, work, or family, and provide information about how to get sufficient sleep regardless.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I actually took a course called Modeling Biological Dynamics with Prof. Rosemary Braun, who is my mentor for this research project, and in that class, we learned mathematical and computational techniques for analyzing and predicting biological dynamics. So much of biology is made up of these dynamic systems, and it is incredible to see how we can model those computationally! It was eye-opening to be able to implement equations into code and see a system "come to life" as I generated the plots on my computer, and further, to be able to change parts of those equations and see how it impacts our system. The course was incredible & solidified my already intense passion for computational biology 🙂 Prof. Braun played a huge role in that, because in lecture she would be just as excited about whatever we were going to cover that day and she went above and beyond in explaining how and why these dynamic models are made and what makes them work. She happened to be starting a new project on modeling individual sleep cycles after our course ended, and reached out to see if any students would like to join - which became the opportunity of a lifetime for me!

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at a conference one day?
I would definitely recommend starting off with an undergraduate conference - a great option being the OUR's Annual Research Expo in the Spring - because it's honestly a lot less nerve-wracking for your first-time presentation to be to mostly undergraduate students who can relate to your current experience. Please provide a brief summary of your research.
Past research in syntax has shown that a phenomenon called "grammatical illusion" exists in English. "Grammatical illusion" happens when native speakers of a language erroneously accept ungrammatical sentences. For example, in "The key to the boxes are on the table" (Bock & Miller, 1991), the plural noun, boxes, makes readers erroneously accept this sentence. More specifially, researchers have found grammatical illusions in English "locative constructions," which refer to sentences like "Mary put chocolates in a container" or "I poured water into the cup" (Kim & Yoshida, 2016). So far, there has been no related research in Mandarin Chinese. In my research, I aim to answer the following questions though studying Chinese locative constructions: Do grammatical illusions exist in Mandarin, or is the phenomenon only observed in English? If it does, in which environments are such illusions most prevalent?

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
Before Winter 2022, I had never thought that I would pursue research in syntax. Although I was already a Linguistics major interested in human language at the time, the connection between language and social factors (sociolinguistics) excited me the most. In Winter 2022, I took Prof. Masaya Yoshida's class on syntax. Hoping to understand the relationship between syntax and sociolinguistics, I went to Masaya's office hours. Little did I know, our discussions opened a new world for me: As a bilingual speaker, how does my Chinese syntax affect my English? How can Chinese and English syntax be similar in unexpected ways? These questions motivated my research questions for this project and drives me to fill the gap in the field of Chinese syntax research.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly?
Research has always been a way to fulfill my curiosity, intellectual or not. It also enables me to explore different facets of my identity in a systematic way. For example, I enjoy watching New Wave films, and I'm also interested in diverse Chinese dialects. Last year, I was able to combine these two interests of mine in my research project "The Use of Languages in Taiwan New Cinema." I was able to watch as many Taiwanese films as I wanted and learn more about how history affected language manifested in the films. Research allows me to dive deeply into my passions, and that's why research has also become one of my passions.

I learned that patience is key, and that it's always important to trust the process.

Please provide a brief summary of your research.

Broadly, my research focuses on testing the antimicrobial properties of different types of materials, both porous and non-porous, and evaluating their potential for usage in real-world environments, such as healthcare facilities and public transportation. Heavy metals such as copper and silver are known to have inherent antimicrobial properties, which has led to recent advancements in copper-coated and metal nanoparticle-containing materials. How environmental factors such as humidity could enhance or diminish the antimicrobial properties of these novel materials is poorly understood. My work aims to establish the antimicrobial efficacy of copper-coated stainless steel and metal nanoparticle-containing textiles under different humidity conditions, as well as determine how bacteria might respond to exposure to these materials. The testing process is actually quite simple: I apply bacteria to the materials in question and allow them to sit on the materials in a specific humidity environment for a given length of time. I then recover the bacteria from the materials and quantify the amount of surviving bacteria relative to the initial amount of bacteria applied. So far, I've found that the antimicrobial efficacies of both copper-coated stainless steel and metal-containing textiles are not significantly affected by changes in humidity. In the future, I will investigate using artificial saliva as the bacteria-containing medium, which contain salts and small molecules known to affect the viability of viruses. Ultimately, these test results will help improve our understanding of when and how to use heavy metal-containing materials in healthcare, commercial, and residential facilities for the benefit of public health, and reveal considerations we should make before replacing traditional materials with antimicrobial ones to prevent transmission of COVID-19 and other pathogens.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?

Public health has always been a special topic of interest for me, and learning about superbugs and antibiotic resistance throughout high school got me really interested in the different "microbiomes" we interact with on a daily basis, whether it be in the air we breathe or in the lids of our water bottles. I wanted to get hands-on experience working with different microbes and become involved in something that could address the spread of antibiotic resistance. This project was the perfect opportunity to do so. The materials I was working with were potential alternatives to using antibiotics on traditional surfaces, and Professor Hartmann's lab had a lot of really interesting bacterial strains gathered from indoor microbial communities.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly?

For me, interdisciplinary research felt like the natural first step in putting the skills I've learned in classes to good use. Because research is so investigative, it has allowed me to take all the knowledge I'd stored in the back of my brain and use it to ask questions and learn even more skills. Unlike the many jobs and internships I was looking into at the time, research was much more amorphous in that I had the freedom to really think about what I wanted to explore and what skills I wanted to gain from my experience.

With wet-lab work, it took me a lot of time to wrap my head around each step of a protocol and understand why I was doing it. Because this was my first time working on a wet-lab project, I think one of the most important skills I learned was to be comfortable asking questions when I wasn't sure about something. Knowing what you are doing and why you are doing it makes research much more enjoyable, and also allows you to learn a variety of different technical skills you might not have otherwise found.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in pursuing undergraduate research?

When finding a research opportunity, make sure you find a project that you are genuinely curious about, not just because it sounds cool or "cutting-edge". Your work might not seem as awesome as someone else's, but you will be much more invested and be able to talk about your research more easily if it's something you are genuinely interested in. Also, when research starts feeling slow because you aren't getting good results or a piece of equipment is down and you can't run a protocol, remind yourself that everyone in research has experienced something similar. Stay optimistic and focused on your project's goals and remember that negative results can be useful as well!

Please provide a brief summary of your research: My research focuses on forecasting dynamical systems, which are systems that change over time, such as vibrations in structures, weather patterns, financial markets, and the spread of diseases. Traditional models often struggle to take full advantage of the large amounts of data available today, and they rarely tell us how reliable their predictions are. To address this, our work develops a new data-driven approach using neural operators, a modern machine learning technique that learns how entire systems evolve over time. Beyond predicting future behavior, our approach also estimates how confident those predictions are by drawing on statistical ideas such as quantile regression and Bayesian methods. This allows the model to capture both errors in the data and limitations in the model itself, producing predictions along with confidence intervals.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular? AI is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily lives, so I was interested in doing something related to machine learning because machine learning is what we use to train AI.

What made you interested in pursuing (interdisciplinary) research more broadly? What drew me to interdisciplinary research is that the problems I find most interesting rarely fit inside a single field. My work on uncertainty quantification for dynamical systems sits at the intersection of machine learning, statistics, and the physical sciences, and it only works because ideas from each inform the others. Coming from computer engineering, I enjoy moving between the theory and the implementation, and I have found that the most useful insights often come from borrowing a concept from one area and applying it somewhere it was not originally meant to go. 

Describe your experiences with research thus far. Was it tricky? What skills do you think you’ve gained? Yes, research takes a lot of time, but it is rewarding in the end. I have developed strong analytical skills, learning how to break down complex problems, question my assumptions, and work through challenges methodically when results do not turn out as expected. Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My research in the Geraci lab looks to implement a Horizontal Fiber Interferometer (HIFO) within the ARIADNE experiment. Within ARIADNE, an experiment searching for a well-motivated dark matter candidate the Axion, a rotating source mass is utilized to generate a pseudo magnetic field carried by the axion, affecting hyper-polarized helium-3 gas. Due to the design and nature of the experiment, the source mass will have a slight wobble to its motion, but this wobble must not exceed 75 microns. A method to detect this, the HIFO, is necessary to readout the displacement of the rotor in situ, under cryogenic vacuum conditions reaching 4K and 10E-6 atm. The HIFO is a laser interferometer which shines perpendicular to the rotating source mass and utilizes a metric known as visibility to detect the wobble. During my past research, it was found that there is a direct one to one relationship between measured visibility and distance from the rotating mass. My past work has also shown this direct relationship can be utilized as a "ruler," precisely measuring the displacement of the source mass on the order of several microns. Over the past year and a half, my research has pursued designing, implementing, testing, and utilizing this HIFO to accurately measure the displacement of the source mass for eventual data taking experimental runs of the larger ARIADNE experiment.

Coming to Northwestern, I knew I was interested in being involved with physics research. As I was looking into different labs, the Geraci group within the Center for Fundamental Physics caught my eye as it had many tabletop physics experiments probing the limits of our knowledge of physics. These conversations made it clear that, although staffing issues and the mental health needs of youth in juvenile correctional settings have been ongoing concerns and topics of academic discussion, there is a noticeable gap in concrete, state-level research. Please provide a brief summary of your research.
A subset of Parkinson's patients face increased aggregation of alpha-synuclein due to loss of activity of Glucosylceramidase (GCase). Our project focuses on increasing GCase activity through a multivalent Spherical Nucleic Acid (SNA) platform, where we used GCase as the protein core and attached Folate and Transferrin on GCase. Folate and Transferrin are both receptors found on the Blood Brain Barrier (BBB), so our hypothesis was that adding both moieties would significantly improve receptor mediated trancytosis of our construct. Our results have shown that the Bivalent Construct (protein construct with both groups) and the Transferrin Construct (protein construct with just Transferrin) had increased activity and uptake results, and the Bivalent Construct showed complete recovery of GCase activity under Parkinson's-like conditions in cells.

What was the most surprising moment of your trip, and why did it resonate with you?
The Philippines is home to roughly 180 languages, around 35 of which are considered endangered. Can you share a compelling insight you discovered through your research that you hadn’t anticipated when designing your proposal?
When I designed my proposal, I knew I wanted to study minority and indigenous language revitalization. However, I hadn’t expected the interpretations of those two words — “minority” and “indigenous”— to be so different around the world. In some of the countries I visited, “indigenous” referred to whoever settled the land first. In others, it seemed to correlate with the largest ethnic group, or even the group most represented in government. Yet in many places, indigenous and minority populations go hand in hand, and their languages are almost never used in government spaces. It was fascinating to compare these distinctions and learn how they influence the everyday lives of different groups in the same community.

Will Yuen

Please provide a brief summary of your research.
My focus was pre-clinical research concerning a promising potential therapeutic to alleviate Renal Ischemic Reperfusion Injury (IRI), an unavoidable injury in the organ transplant setting. There are currently no effective treatments for this inevitable injury. To do this my lab and I developed a novel in vitro cold hypoxia and reperfusion protocol to best model transplant related IRI in tubular epithelial cells (TECs), the main target of this type of injury. This involved subjecting TECs to 6h of cold hypoxia followed by a designated time of reperfusion (incubation in fresh media at 37C). My research confirmed that this model properly mimicked renal IRI in vitro by confirming the presence of inflammation, kidney injury, and cell death in TECs via qPCR, flow cytometry, and fluorescence staining assays across multiple time points (0h, 2h, 16h, and 24h of reperfusion) compared to control. I then investigated the effect of the potential therapeutic on these same factors. The therapeutic is an siRNA knockdown of XBP1, a vital transcription factor in the ER stress pathway that results in inflammation. Compared to non-transfected cells, TECs transfected with XBP1 siRNA displayed less inflammation, kidney injury, and cell death imaged/quantified via the same assays used previously. This emphasized that the knockdown of XBP1 in TECs is a promising potential therapeutic to alleviate IRI.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I found it particularly compelling that this type of injury (IRI) is quite unavoidable during/after transplantation and that we somehow have not developed any effective solutions to this injury. This pattern extended across many participants' interpersonal interactions, experiences with institutional systems (e.g., medical leave, accommodations), and understandings of embedded cultural norms and power relations within academia. In my paper and presentation, I also identified several concrete ways that academics can create more accessible, anti-oppressive PhD environments, based on participants' narratives. This made it especially exciting to share my findings with an audience of higher education researchers and practitioners who wanted to learn about supporting this particular group.

What made you initially interested in researching your project in particular?
I began with a broad interest in how disability is constructed and treated within academia, particularly after reading about the concept of "academic ableism." This concept describes the ways in which structures and practices in higher education often marginalize disabled people, regardless of conscious intentions. A lot of research on disability in academia has focused on undergraduates, with a growing body of literature exploring faculty experiences, but I found very little work that centered PhD students. I thought this was a critical gap, given that PhD programs operate as an important gateway to academic careers. The focus on chronic illness specifically came from my interest in exploring healthcare access as part of accessibility in higher education. Chronic illnesses are distinct in that they often necessitate ongoing medical support, but conversations about disability access in higher education often just focus on the classroom.

What conference(s) did you present at and how did you find out about them?
I presented at the American Education Research Association's 2024 Annual Meeting in Philadelphia. I was fortunate to learn about the opportunity from a mentor (formerly at the Office of Undergraduate Research!) with expertise in research on higher education. Having this mentor's support throughout the whole process definitely helped me have a positive experience with the conference.

What was it like presenting at a conference? Anything that you didn't expect?
My presentation was a paper session, which meant that I gave a 15 minute talk to an audience as part of a small panel. To be honest, I was terrified for this presentation for weeks leading up to the conference. What gave me the ability to not only give my talk but also communicate in a way that I felt proud of was remembering the purpose of research (in my opinion) - that is, to share it with others to help drive material, justice-oriented change. One thing I didn't expect was the overwhelmingly supportive and engaged response that my presentation was met with. As an undergraduate, I wasn't sure how I would interact with an audience of more advanced scholars and professionals, but they really treated my ideas with earnestness.

Any tips or advice you have for students similar to you that are interested in presenting at a conference one day?
First, try to push back against any imposterization that you feel - you have valuable ideas to share, and you're worthy of giving yourself this opportunity. I never thought I would be capable of this kind of presentation, but having this chance to push myself showed me that being afraid and uncomfortable isn't the same thing as being unable or undeserving. Second, don't be afraid to draw upon your support network throughout the whole process, from identifying a conference, crafting your submission, using the submission portal, registration/logistics, practicing your presentation, and navigating the conference itself. Conferences can be intimidating, but having guidance from your professors, academic advisors, OUR staff, peers, and family can make a huge difference.
